_comment: Curated topology alternatives. Each entry is a question with two or more
answers; the app shows them as a toggle and rewrites the tree live.
An answer is a list of operations applied to the reference tree, so the payload
carries one tree and a few hundred bytes of rearrangement instructions rather
node:Gnathostomata            a backbone id from backbone.json
fossil:Arthrodira             a fossil id from fossils.json
mrca:Homo_sapiens,Mus_musculus   the MRCA of those living tips
spr      move a clade to become sister to another node. If the target is an
ancestor of the moved clade, the clade becomes sister to the
remainder of that group, which is how 'X branches off first' is
cluster  gather several separate lineages into one clade and attach it. This
is what turns a grade back into a monophyletic group.
Every non-default answer marks the affected branches as schematic: the
rearranged topology is real but the node ages have not been re-estimated under
it, and the app says so.

alternatives.label: Where do turtles go?
alternatives.blurb: Turtles have no temporal fenestrae, which for a century put them outside the diapsids entirely. Molecular data put them with archosaurs. Almost every possible answer has been the consensus at some point.

options.label: Sister to archosaurs
options.note: Recovered by essentially all large molecular datasets. The fenestrae were lost secondarily.
refs: Crawford et al. 2015 Mol Phylogenet Evol 83:250

options.label: Sister to crocodilians
options.note: An early mitochondrial result, now abandoned. Long-branch attraction is the usual explanation.

options.label: Sister to lizards and tuatara
options.note: Recovered by some nuclear analyses and by microRNA data.

options.label: Outside all other reptiles
options.note: The morphological default through most of the twentieth century, from the absent temporal openings. No molecular dataset supports it.

alternatives.label: Where is the root of placental mammals?
alternatives.blurb: Three living superorders, three possible rootings, and the branch separating them is short enough that this has stayed open for twenty years.

options.label: Afrotheria + Xenarthra together
options.note: Favoured by the largest genomic datasets including Zoonomia. Consistent with a Gondwanan origin.

options.label: Afrotheria branches off first
options.note: Recovered by several retroposon and indel analyses.

options.label: Xenarthra branches off first
options.note: The traditional morphological arrangement.

alternatives.label: Where do living amphibians come from?
alternatives.blurb: Frogs, salamanders and caecilians are unambiguously each other's closest living relatives on molecular data. Which Palaeozoic group they came out of is not settled, and one hypothesis says they did not all come out of the same one.

options.label: All three from temnospondyls
options.note: The majority position. Gerobatrachus and the dissorophoid temnospondyls supply the intermediate morphology.

options.label: All three from lepospondyls
options.note: Argued mainly from large morphological matrices, and it implies a much younger crown Tetrapoda.

options.label: Caecilians from a different group
options.note: Frogs and salamanders from temnospondyls, caecilians from lepospondyls. Incompatible with every molecular dataset, which recovers Lissamphibia as a clade with strong support. Included because it is the clearest case in the tree where morphology and molecules give incompatible answers.

alternatives.label: Which two amphibian orders are closest?
alternatives.blurb: Given that Lissamphibia is a clade, the internal arrangement is a second question.

options.label: Frogs + salamanders
options.note: The molecular consensus and the arrangement in the tree as downloaded.

options.label: Salamanders + caecilians
options.note: Recovered by some early nuclear analyses, both of them elongate and limb-reduced. Generally read as a long-branch artefact.

alternatives.label: Are the ratites a clade?
alternatives.blurb: Ostriches, rheas, emus, cassowaries and kiwi are all large and flightless. Tinamous fly. If the flightless ones form a clade, flight was lost once; if tinamous are nested among them, it was lost repeatedly.

options.label: No — tinamous nest inside
options.sublabel: flight lost at least four times
options.note: Tinamous group with the extinct moa, and elephant birds group with kiwi. Both results come from ancient DNA and both break ratite monophyly.

options.label: Yes — ratites are a clade
options.note: The traditional arrangement, and the one that made ratite distributions look like a clean Gondwanan vicariance story. It is not supported.

alternatives.label: What branches off first among squamates?
alternatives.blurb: Morphology and molecules disagree about the deepest split in the lizard tree, and the disagreement is not subtle.

options.label: Dibamids and geckos first
options.note: Every large sequence dataset recovers Iguania nested with snakes and anguimorphs.

options.label: Iguania first
options.note: From tongue and feeding morphology: iguanians are lingual feeders, the rest are not. The character is real; whether it is ancestral is the question.
refs: Estes et al. 1988; Conrad 2008 Bull Am Mus Nat Hist 310:1

alternatives.label: Are hagfish and lampreys sister taxa?
alternatives.blurb: Hagfish lack vertebrae, eyes with lenses, and much else. Either they never had them, or they lost them.

options.label: Yes — Cyclostomata
options.note: Supported by microRNAs, phylogenomics, and the fossil Myxinikela, which has pigmented eyes.

options.label: No — lampreys are closer to us
options.note: The morphological reading, in which hagfish are primitively simple rather than degenerate. It makes hagfish the most informative animal alive about the vertebrate ancestor, which is why the question mattered so much.

alternatives.label: Which fish is our closest living relative?
alternatives.blurb: Two lineages of lobe-finned fishes survive. Only one of them can be sister to tetrapods.

options.label: Lungfishes
options.note: The consistent phylogenomic answer.
refs: Irisarri et al. 2017 Nat Ecol Evol 1:1370

options.label: Coelacanths
options.note: The popular assumption after Latimeria was found in 1938, and not what the sequence data say.

options.label: Both, equally
options.note: Recovered occasionally, usually when taxon sampling is thin.

alternatives.label: Are "placoderms" a clade?
alternatives.blurb: This is the toggle that shows what a grade actually is. Switch it and watch eight separate stem lineages collapse into one triangle.

options.label: No — a grade on the gnathostome stem
options.note: Entelognathus has the marginal jaw bones of a bony fish while still being armoured like a placoderm, which places some placoderms closer to Osteichthyes than to other placoderms.

options.label: Yes — a monophyletic Placodermi
options.note: Grouped on shared dermal armour. The armour is now generally read as ancestral for jawed vertebrates rather than diagnostic of a clade.

alternatives.label: Are "acanthodians" a clade?
alternatives.blurb: Same question, different grade, and it moved in the opposite direction: acanthodians went from stem bony fishes to stem cartilaginous fishes.

options.label: No — a grade on the chondrichthyan stem

alternatives.label: What are mosasaurs closest to?
alternatives.blurb: An extinct marine radiation placed inside a living clade, which is the case the scaffold has to handle if fossils are going to be more than decoration.

options.label: Monitor lizards and kin
options.note: The arrangement recovered when a molecular scaffold constrains the living taxa.

options.label: Snakes
options.note: Recovered by morphology-only analyses, and tied up with whether snakes originated in water.
refs: Lee 1997 Phil Trans R Soc B 352:53
